description: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 web framework for .NET 8+, built from scratch. Allocation-conscious routing, a custom HTTP/2 implementation with HPACK, WebSockets, TLS with per-listener ALPN and certificate rotation, response caching, rate limiting and OpenAPI generation.
releaseNotes:
v2.7.0: Three correctness fixes, one of them security-relevant, and substantially less work per request.

Rate limiting counted every client against a single shared allowance. HttpRequest.RemoteIpAddress was null on every HTTP/1.1 request, plaintext and TLS alike, so the limiter's partition key fell through to "unknown" for every caller and one noisy client could exhaust the limit for all of them. X-Forwarded-For never applied either, because the trusted-proxy check is only consulted when the peer address is known. Present since rate limiting shipped in 2.5.0. The cause was ordering: the address was written onto the request before it was parsed, and the parser resets the request at the top of every attempt, because a request can arrive across any number of reads. The connection's facts are now applied after a successful parse. HttpRequest.IsHttps, which was always false on HTTP/1.1 including over TLS, had the same cause and is fixed with it.

304 and HEAD responses sent content. A response can hold its content four ways and both places that suppress it cleared only one, so an endpoint returning an object had it serialized and sent anyway. RFC 9110 15.4.5 forbids content on a 304 and 9.3.2 on a response to HEAD, but the framing was worse: neither carries a length, so the content that followed was read by the peer as the start of the next response and every exchange after it on that connection was misaligned.

HTTP/3 corrupted any header name outside the QPACK static table. The decoder began reading one byte late and took the length byte as the pattern, so the Huffman flag and the length were both wrong and every field after it was misaligned. A client sending an API key or correlation id over HTTP/3 had it silently mangled.

Behaviour change: a connection now parses all of its requests into one HttpRequest, as it already did for responses. A reference kept past the end of a handler will be seen to change, and then to be reused by the next request on that connection or by a different peer once the connection is pooled. Copy what is needed rather than passing the request into background work.

HTTP/2 advertises less to a single peer: SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS drops from 256 to 100 and SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE from 1 MB to 96 KB, both matching Kestrel. Their product is what one peer can oblige the server to buffer, per connection, so this moves the exposure from 256 MB to under 32 MB.

Also on HTTP/3: a request now reports its version as HTTP/3 rather than HTTP/2, which both protocols previously claimed because they share one conversion; the response field section is encoded straight from the response rather than through a list and a string per value; and the end-of-stream flag is sent with the response rather than in a second call to the transport. The last two changed allocation but not throughput, which is worth saying rather than implying otherwise.

Performance: HTTP/1.1 allocates about a third less per request, 1,452 bytes down to 1,030 end to end, by matching methods, versions and known field names against constants the server already holds, building the entity tag in one allocation rather than four, and building the route table's span-keyed lookups once rather than per request. HTTP/3 throughput is 2.9x what it was, 158,621 to 455,556 req/s on sixteen pinned cores, which puts it ahead of Kestrel's own entry at 323,335 on the same host. Two causes: every request made three to five separate reads before it was parsed, because a variable-length integer needs its first byte before its length is known, and every read and write was handed the server's shutdown token, so thousands of concurrent streams contended on one registration lock twice per operation. Frames now come through a buffer, and per-stream operations take no token, which is also what Kestrel does.

v2.6.0: Multiple listeners, cleartext HTTP/2, and certificate rotation without a restart. AddListener() adds a socket beyond UsePort() and UseHttpsPort(), each with its own certificate and its own ALPN list, so one server can advertise HTTP/2 and HTTP/1.1 on one port while advertising HTTP/1.1 alone on another. Per RFC 7301 3.2 the server selects from what the client advertised and its own preference governs, so that list decides what a listener serves. UseHttp2Cleartext serves HTTP/2 with prior knowledge (RFC 9113 3.3), validating the 3.4 connection preface as the TLS path does, so a client speaking HTTP/1.1 on such a port is rejected rather than quietly served. TlsOptions.ReloadOnChange resolves the certificate per handshake through ServerCertificateSelectionCallback, so a renewal on disk takes effect on the next handshake while established connections keep the certificate they negotiated with; the files are polled rather than watched, because renewal tools rename a new pair over the old one and inotify reports that unreliably across container filesystems. Fixes: a header line whose CRLF was split across two TCP reads was answered 400 rather than carried, though RFC 9110 15.5.1 reserves 400 for a client error and where a read ended is not one; a WebSocket reply was held back by a partly-arrived following frame, because the write-batching test asked whether bytes remained rather than whether a whole frame had, and RFC 6455 5.2 frames carry an explicit length; and TLS connections now send a close_notify alert before closing, which RFC 8446 6.1 requires and SslStream.DisposeAsync does not do, without which a truncated response is indistinguishable from a complete one. The alert is sent before the request pipes are completed, because on the HTTP/1.1 path those are created over the SslStream with leaveOpen false and completing either disposes it, and it is bounded by a timeout because ShutdownAsync accepts no CancellationToken.

v2.5.0: Rate limiting. UseRateLimiting() applies a token-bucket allowance per client IP across HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, returning 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After and a ProblemDetails body. Applied before routing, so static files, the OpenAPI document, and floods at nonexistent paths are covered. [RateLimit(PermitLimit, WindowSeconds)] gives an endpoint its own tighter allowance and [DisableRateLimit] exempts one entirely. X-Forwarded-For is honored only from configured trusted proxies, walking the chain right-to-left. Tracked clients are capped so rotating source addresses cannot exhaust memory. Also adds HttpRequest.RemoteIpAddress and 429 to the cached status lines.

v2.4.0: OpenAPI/Swagger integration. UseOpenApi() serves an OpenAPI 3.0.3 document at /openapi/v1.json and Swagger UI at /swagger, generated once at startup from the route table and served from a pre-built buffer, so there is no per-request cost. Routes, path parameter types, request bodies, response schemas, and content types are inferred from existing metadata; [OpenApiOperation], [OpenApiResponse], [OpenApiParameter], and [OpenApiIgnore] add what cannot be. Schema property names follow the server's JsonSerializerOptions and DataAnnotations become schema constraints. Security schemes match the built-in JWT and API-key handlers. Also adds Router.GetRegisteredRoutes() and EndpointInvoker.ResponseType.

v2.3.0: Response caching. UseResponseCaching() serves repeat GET/HEAD requests from a bounded in-process store, skipping endpoint execution and JSON serialization, and emits Cache-Control/Vary/Age for client and proxy caches. Opt-in per endpoint via [ResponseCache(Duration, Location, VaryByHeader, VaryByQueryKeys)]. Entries expire on their duration and are evicted when a successful POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE hits the same path. Cache hits answer If-None-Match with 304 on HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. Requests carrying Authorization bypass the shared cache unless the endpoint opts in. Also fixes HTTP/2 outbound flow control: the send path now honors the peer's stream- and connection-level send windows (RFC 7540 6.9) instead of queueing whole bodies at once, and the connection send window starts at the RFC default of 65535 with the client's SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE tracked separately.
